IS : 5864 � 1983

Indian Standard
METHODS FOR DETERMINATION OF DDT RESIDUES IN FOOD COMMODITIES

( First Revision)
o.
FOR E W 0 R 0

0.1 This Indian Standard (First Revision) was adopted by the Indian Standards Institution on 30 August 1983, after the draft finalized by the Pesticides Residue Analysis Sectional Comrmttee had been approved by the Agricultural and Food PI od ucts Division Council. 0.2 DDT formulations are popular in agriculture and public health for the control of various insect pests and vectors of diseases, Frequent and increased use of these for mu lations often result in harmful effect due to toxic nature of their residues. Careful assessment of residues is therefore, an important step in safcguar ding human health and in the establishment of sound regulatory policy.

0.3 This standard was first published as IS: 5864 (Part 1) - 1970� covering determ in.ition of DDT residues in food grains and their milled products. The present revision includes other food commodities not covered earlier and incorporates more sensitive gas chromatographic method. For qualitative confirmation of residues, thin layer chromatography has also been prescribed.
0.4 This standard will enable the health authorities and others to follow uniform test procedure for the estimation of DDT residues in various foods. 0.5 In reporting the result of a test or analysis made in accordance with this standard, if the final value, observed or calculated, is to be rounded off, it shall be done in accordance with IS : 2 - 1960t.
-Method for determination of DDT residues: Part I Foodgrains and their milled products. tRules for rounding off numerical values (revised).

3

IS: 5864� 1983
1. SCOPE 1.1 This standard prescribes gas chromatographic and spectrophotometric methods for the determination of DDT [2, 2-bis (p-chlorophenyl) - I, I, l-trichloroethane and related isomers] residues in foods.

1.1.1 The gas chromatographic method determines residues of p,p' �DDT and related isomers such as p,p' -DDE [2,2-bis (p-chlorophenyl) I-I-dichloroethylene], p,p' -TDE [ 2,2-bis (p-chlorophenyl) I,l-dichloroethane J and o,p' -DDT [2 - (p-chlorophenyl) 2- ( o-chlorophenyl ) - I, I, l-t richloroethane ] in the range of 0'0 I to 0'02 ~g/g (0'01 to 0'02 ppm ), whereas the limit of detection with spectrophotometric method is 0'1 to 0'3 Ilgjg (0'1 to 0'3 ppm).
1.1.2 The procedures based on the use of alternate GLC column, thin layer chromatography and microalkali derivatization are also being prescribed for the confirmation of the nature of DDT residues. 2. SAMPLING 2.1 The respresentative sample for the purpose of DDT residues in foods shall be in accordance with the sampling procedures as prescribed in the relevant Indian Standards, wherever available.
2.2 Preparation of the Laboratory Sample

2.2.1 Cereals, Pulses, Spires, Condiments, Tea,

2.2.2 VegetabLes and Fruits
a) Remove visible soil particles by gentle rubbing. Root vegetables may need scrubbing with a brush and some washing. b) Remove all inedible portions of vegetables, such as outer leaves of cabbage, carrot tops, stems of tomatoes, stems and stones of fruits, etc. c) If a peel or skin is not normally consumed, it should be removed ( for example, peas, oranges) and if edible, then it should be included ( for example, carrot, potatoes ). d) Cut a representative sample into pieces and reduce by mixing and quartering to about 300 g. e) Blend the 300-g sample in a waring blender to obtain homogeneous mixture. Mix contents with spatula and reblend to ensure homogeniety. 4

IS : 5864 � 1983
2.2.3 Oilseeds and Nuts a) Remove and discard shells, if present. b) Reduce the sample by mixing and quartering to the desired sample size needed for extraction. Chop finely.
2.2.4 Fats as Butter, Ghee, Cream. etc

a) Melt the sample and filte r to separate oil from other solids which may be present. b) Store the sample in a refrigerator. c) Cut the sample into small cubes. d) Place cubes ( weighing 25 g) in a beaker and heat at 50�C for the oil to sepdrate. 2.2.5 Vegetable Oils (Hydrogenated and Ullhydrogenated) need any sample preparation.

2.2.10 Water arid Beverages - These do not need any processing. 2.3 Storage of Samples - Store samples as such or if the bulk is too much, after preparation of the laboratory sample. Depending upon the nature, store the samples either in deep-freezer (-15�C) or in refrigerator ( 4�C) until taken up for analysis. Ensure that the samples do not absorb or lose moisture during storage. Avoid undue long storage periods.

3.3 Extraction and Partitioning
a) As the extraction and partitiomng schemes are based on moisture, Iat and sugar content of the foods, it is suggested that , The Nutritive Value of Irid ian Foods and the Planning of Satisfactory DIet' by W R. Aykr oyd; published by the Indian Council of Medical Rese.irch, New Delhi or other suitable food composition rables may be consulted to find moisture, fat and sugar content of various food commodities. b) If some s.i mplr; extracts are difficult to filter ( wheat flour, rice, bananas) or there is an emulsion formation during partitioning, obtain a clear solution by centrifuging at 3000 rev/min for 10 minutes or rnor e,

3.3.1 Non-Fatty Foods - Less than 2 percent fat content. 3.3.1.1 Commodities with more than 75 prrce�! moisture and less than 5 percent sligar content - For example most of the' ('!5ctables and some of the fruits. Extract 50 g sample twice with J 00 ml and 50 ml methyl cyanide by blending for 3 minutes each. FIlter the extracts through Buchner funnel using Whatm,tn No. I or equivalent filter paper under vacuum. Transfer the filter-ate into l-Iin e separatory funnel, dilute with 600 ml of 5 percent aqueous sodium chloride and partiuon twice with 100 ml portions of n-hexane. Combine n-hcx ane layer, dry over anhydrous sodium sulphate and concentrate on <t rotary vacuum evaporator or Kuderna-Danish evaporator to about 10 ml. 3.3.1.2 Commodities with more than 75 percent moisture and sugar greater than 5 percent - For example, grapes and banana, etc. Use methyl cyanide: water ( 2 : I v(v ) as extraction solvent and proceed as in 3.3.1.1. 3.3.1.3 Commodities with less than 75 percent moisture - For example cereals, pulses, condiments, tea leaves, coffee and salt. Extract 50 g sample with 100 ml ( or enough to thoroughly wet the sample) portions of methyl cyanide: water ( 2 : 1 vlv) mixture by blending for 3 minutes each and proceed further as in 3.3.1.1.

3.3.1.4 Water and beverages - For example, drinking water, soft drinks, tea and coffee infusions. Partition twice 1 litre sample with 100 ml portions of n-hexane , combine the r,-hcxane layers, dry over anhydrous sodium sulphate and concentrate on a rotary vacuum or Kuderna-Danish evaporator to about 10 ml. 3.3.2 Fatty Foods - Mare than 2 percent fat content. 3.3.2.1 Oils and Fats - Take 15 g sample, divide it into three 5-g sub-samples and dissol ve in 100, 15 and 1:) ml portions of n-hexane. 3.3.2.2 Milk - Take 100 ml milk in the blender, add 100 ml each of acetone and s-hexane and blend for ~ minutes. Transfer homogenate into centrifuge bottle'> and centrifuge at 2000 rpm for 10 minutes. Take upper organic phase in a SOO-ml separatory funnel and re-extract the lower layer twice with 100 ml portions of n-hexane and collect as before. Was h the combined n-he xano phase twice with ~oo ml portions of distilled water. Dry the combined upper n-hexane phase over anhydrous sodium sulphate and concentrate to about 100 ml on rotary vacuum evaporator or Kuderna-Danish evaporative concentrator (Jee Fig. 2 ). 3.3.2.3 Meat, eg!;s, nuls , oilseeds, curd, cheese, etc - Take suitable Sample size (10 to 50 g ) cont.iinmg less rh.m 5 g fat and proceed as in 3.3.2.2. 3.4 Clean-up
3.4.1 For Non-Fait} Foods - Take the concentrated n-hcxane extract (see 3.3.1) in a 25-ml sep.iratory funnel and add concentrated sulphuric acid drop wise with a pipette till the upper n-hexane layer becomes clear. Discard the 10'-'\ er phase of spent sulphuric acid and wash the upper layer with three 10-ml portions of distilled water. Concentrate the n-hexane phase to the desired volume using either Micro-Snyder column or gentle steam of nitrogen. In genl'ral, 50 g samples of cereais, pulses, vegetables, fruits and 1 litre water and beverages will require about 15 ml sulphuric acid.

4. GAS-CHROMATOGRAPHIC METHOD

4.1 Principle - The extracted DDT residue are measured using a gas-chromatograph equipped with electron capture detector. The amount of the residues is measured by comparing the sample response with the response of the standards. 4.2 Apparatus
4.2.1 Gar-Chromatograph - Appropriate gas-chromatograph equipped with electron-capture detector (3H or 83Ni). The suggested operating conditions are:

a) Column - A column made of borosilicate glass, 1'8 m long, 4 mm LD. and packed with any of the appropriate materials given below or their equivalents:

1) I'S percent OV-17/1'95 percent OV-21O liquid phases premixed and coated on silanized Gas Chrom Q80/100 mesh. 2) 4 percent SE-30/6 percent OV -210 liquid phases premixed and coated on silanized Gas Chrorn Q 80/100 mesh.
b) Injection port temperature

c) Column over temperature d) Detector temperature e) Carrier gas ( flow rate) 4.3 Reagents

220"C
Ultra-high 70 mlJmin pure nitrogen,

4.3.1 Working standard mixture containing p.p'-DDE, P,p'-TDE o,p'DDT and P,p'-DDT at the concentration of 0'2, 0'4, 0-4 and 0'4 IJg/ml respectively in n-hexane.
4.3.2 Solution containingp,p'-DDE 1 Ilg/ml each of at the concentration of 0'2 ug/m1 in a-hexane.

4.3.3 Standard mixture containing l/-,g,'1II1 each of p,p'.DDE,p,p'.TDE D,p'-DDT and p,p'�DDT in acetone.

4.4 Procedure - The column is conditioned and evaluated following the
standard procedure, before actual use for analysis. The operating parameter s are set to obtain about half-scale deflection with 1 -s p,p'-DDE (see 4.3.2). Inject standard mixture with the component pesticides ( see 4.3.1 ) at three concentration levels with a microlitre syringe. Inject 3- 8-141 of the clean-up sample extract so that the injection volume contains about 400 mg sample equivalents of water and beverages or 20 mg of all other samples. If necessary, dilute the extract suitably so that the peak heights of sample and standards do not vary more than 25 percent. Identify the residues by comparing the retention times of the sample peaks with those of the pesticides standards.

4.6 Expression of Result - Express DDT residues as the sum of p,p'�DDT, o,p'-DDT, p,p'-DDE and p,p'�TDE in the sample as IJg/g ( ppm).
NOTE Quantify only the peaks which give gr<'ater than 10 percent full-scale deflection ( FSD ) when the sample equivalent to 400 rng in the case of water and beverages and 20 mg in the case of others, arc inj<'ct('d in GLC. Indicate the compounds which produce peaks less than 10 percent FSO as tract (T). If at the retention time of compound, signal is not distinguishable from background, indicate it as not detectable (NO).

4.7 Assuring the Reliability of the Analysis - Pesticides residue analysis involves the determination of the minute quantities of the various compounds in several substrates. Such trace analysis has certain inherent
11

IS : 5864 � 1983
difficulties and the reliability of the analytical method should be assured by following the proced ure ~iven in 4.7.1. Take four samples of the size as recommended under 3.3 and fortify three of these at the level of 2'5 ppm in case of water and beverages, and 0'05 ppm In the case of other commodities by adding appropriate volume of standard mixture (see 4.3.3). Process all tile 4 samples following the suitable procedures ( see 3 and 4). The recovery of Various residues over the background values obtained from unfortified sam pie should be above 80 percent of the added compounds. The difference between the recoveries fr orn the fortified replicates should be � 20 percent.
NOTE - If the background values of t he rt's,dlll's in the sample are. xpected to be high, increase the level 01 for uficauon 10 dOOUlcloubk of the ""P' ct ed background levels.

5. SPECTROPHOTOMETRIC METHOD
5.1 Principle - The cleaned up sample extract is niu ated with nitric acid-sulphuric acid mixture to obtain tctr.min o derivative which is then extracted in ether-petroleum ether rrnxtu re, dried, taken in benzene and treated with sodium rnerhoxide to get blue colour whose absorbence is measured at 600 nm. The amount of DDT in sample is calculated from the standard curve prepared from pure p,p' -DDT. 5.2 Apparatus

5.2.1 Spectrophotometer
5.3 Reagents

5.3.1 Benzme -- Thiophene Free 5.3.2 Ether-Petroleum Ether MIxture - Prepare by nllxmg one part of peroxide and aldehyde free ether with four parts of redistilled petroleum ether. 5.3.3 Nitrating ",..fixture - Prepare fresh mixture everytime by mixing equal volumes of fuming nitric acid (r.d. 1'5) and sulphuric acid ( r.d. 1'84). 5.3.4 Oleic Acid 5.3.5 Reference Standards
5.3.5.1 10 ugjml P,p'-DDT in benzene. 5.3.5.2 10ugjml p,p'�DDT in acetone.

12

IS : 5864 � 1983
5.3.6 Sodium Hydroxide 10 percent aqueous solution.

5.3.7 Sodium Methoxide - 10 percent, prepare by refluxing 20 gm freshly cut sodium with 500 ml anhydrous methanol; cool, centrifuge and dilute the supernatant with anhydrous methanol. Adjust batches of sodium methoxide to exact concentration by titration with standard acid. Store in dispensing systems excluding carbon dioxide and moisture. Prepare new standard curve for every batch of sodium methoxide, 5.4 Preparation of Standard Curve ( 0 - 50 Itg Range) -- Take 0, 10, 20,30,40,50 IJg p,p'-DDT in benzene (see 5.3.5.1) in 50-011 Erlenmeyer flask, add 10 mg oleic acid in benzene to each flask and evaporate to dryness by a gentle stream of dry air. Chill the flask in an ice-bath and to each add 5 011 chilled nitrating mixture. Swirl the flasks to wet all the portions of the residues and heat on a steam bath for one hour.

5.4.1 Cool and transfer the contents of an Erlenmeyer flask to 125-ml separatory funnel using three 20-ml portions of ice cold distilled water. Rinse the flask with two :lO-ml portions of ether petroleum ether mixture, add these rinsings to the separatory funnel and re-extract it with 20 ml of ether-petroleum ether mixture. Combine the ether-petroleum ether layers and wash first with two IO-ml portions of aqueous 10 percent sodium hydroxide and then with two 20�ml portions of aqueous saturated sodium chloride. Transfer it to a 2.'>0-ml Erlenmyer flask through 1 ern thick layer of anhydrous sodium sulphate previously wetted with etherpetroleum ether mixture. Rinse the separatory funnel with two l O-ml portions of ether-petroleum ether mixture and transfer these rinsings also to the flask. Evaporate the contents in the Erlenmeyer flask to dryness on a steam bath. Cool the flask, dissolve the residue in 3 ml benzene and add 6 ml sodium methoxide. Mix thoroughly and after 15 minutes, measure absorbance at 600 n m against benzene and sodium methoxide ( I : 2 viv ) solution. Plot absorbance against fLg DDT to obtain standard curve.
5.5 Q.uantitation of DDT in the Sample - Add 10 mg oleic acid in benzene to the cleaned-up sample extract and evaporate the contents to dryness on a steam bath. Proceed further as for preparation for standard curve as described in 5.4. If absorbance is greater than 0'8, dilute suitably with benzene to get a value in the range of 0'2 to 0'8. Calculate p,p'-DDT in the sample using standard curve. Also measure absorbance at 510 nm and calculate p,p' -DOE using two colour component system. 5.6 Expression of Results - Express the residues in the samples as Ilg(g (ppm).

5.7 Assuring the Reliability of the Analysis - Proceed as in 4.7.1 except that fortify the samples at the level of 0'025 ppm in the case
13

IS 15864 - 1983 of water and beverages and O-S ppm in the case of other commodities by adding appropriate volume of' standar d solution of p,p'-DDT in acetone ( Set 5.3.5.2) and process the samples following the suitable procedure outlined in 3 and 5.

6. CONFIRMATION OF THE RESIDUES
6.1 The identity of pesticide residues detected and tentatively identified by gas-liquid chromatographic (GLC) method needs confirmation. Depending on the nature and level of the residues, select one or more of the following confirmatory procedures. 6.2 Alternate GLC ColulDn - The elution pattern of organochlorine insecticide residues on a column packed with 3 percent DEGS on Gas Chrom Q is quite different from other generally used columns. This column may be used for quick confirmation of the low levels of the insecticide residues. 6.3 Thin-Layer Chromatography (TLC) - Prepare 0 25 mm thick alumina G plates impregnated with about 40 mg silver nitrate per plate. Air dry a plate, activate it at 110�C for 45 minutes and cool it. Spot insecticide standard mixture ( about 0-02 ml of 10 IJg,'ml solution of each of /J,p'-DDE, P,!I'. TDE, p,p'-DDT and o,p'-DDT) and suitable aliquots of cleaned-up extracts. Develop the plate up to 12 to 15 cm in a saturated chamber, using suitable developing solvent, such as heptane, n-hexane or mixture of n-hexane and benzene (1-: 1 vlv). Air dry and expose the plate to ultra-violent light for about 30 minutes, when the insecticides residues will appear as black spots. Identify the residues by comparing the Rf values with those of the standards co-chromatographed. 6.4 Micro-alkali Derivatisation - Take 5 ml aliquot of cleaned-up n-hexane extract having residue concentrations suitable for GLC analysis in a 15-ml graduated tube. Add 2 ml ethanolic KOH and beat in a water bath at SO�C for 2 hours. Add more n-hexane when the solution in the tube nears drying. Remove the tube from the water bath, cool, and add 5 ml ethanol: water ( 1 : 1 v,'v) and 2 ml hexane, stopper and shake gently. Allow the layers to separate and inject suitable aliquots of n-hexane phase into GLe. Conform disappearance or shifts in the peak pattern in alkali derivatized sample as compared to underivatized sample. By this treatment, p,p'-DDE, o,p'-DDT and P,P'- TDE will change to p,p'-DDE, o,p'-DDE and DDMU, respectively, while p,p'-DDE will not be affected. 6.5 Interferences Due to Polychlorinated Biphenyls - Polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) are industrial chemicals which are used in manufacture of synthetic rubber, electrical products, printing inks, paints, 14

Is : 5864 � 1983
varnishes, resins, etc. These are resistant 10 oxidation and reduction and thus, like DDT residues, are widely drstr rbured in the environment. Being polychlorinated biphenyls, these h ave physical and che nncal properties of chlorinated hydrocarbon msecucidc residues and thus a method of ana lysis of DDT and BBC will also detect PCBs. In addrnon to the environmental contamination of the sample, PC B~ from rubber and from rubber and plastic caps and lmmg of the cont a mers and laboratory apparatus can cause interferences On GLC, PCBs produce mulripIe pe aks some of which may have s.irne retentron times as t ha t of BRC and DDT residues. So due care should be taken to avoid the contact of the samples during collecuon, storage and analysis with rubber or plastics. 6.5.1 If a sample gives multiple peaks on GLC (as Will be the case with a sample containmg both BHC and DDT residues ), the absence or prf'sence of PCBs can be confir rne d by rnicro-alkah treatment ( see 6.4).

If after treatment with alk.ih, the peaks on GLC corresponding to p,p'-TDE, p,p'-DDT and HHl ivomers are completely eliminated, it would indicate absence of PCBs If then' IS only pal tra] or no decrease 10 the peaks heights, sample ma y be containmg PCBs. If the suspected PCBs level is fair ly high, t herr presence ran be further confirmed by TLC (su 6.3), when the alkali derrvanzed sample Will giVe at the most 2 spots (one near the soh ent and a nothr-r corresponding to p,p'-DDT ), rather than giving several spots correspondrng to Rf values of BHr and DDT residues.
